Birds are processed at the table in the order they came out of the net, ringed, aged, sexed where
possible, measured and weighed, and released within minutes from the release box facing the
marsh. Nothing is held for a photograph beyond the record shot the recorder takes, and a bird that
shows any sign of stress is released at once with whatever data has been taken and the word
stressed in the notes column.

The ringing data go into the ledger at the table in pencil, are checked against the rings used before
the session closes, and are typed into the national database within the week by whoever kept the
ledger. A total that does not reconcile with the rings used is investigated on the day, however late it
makes everyone, because a missing ring is either a bird ringed twice or a ring lost on the marsh, and
both matter to the scheme and to us.

Recoveries, which here means rings reported from elsewhere or found on birds caught here that
were ringed somewhere else, are the most exciting post the observatory gets and are written up on
the noticeboard the day they arrive, with a map. The oldest recovery on the board is a turnstone
ringed in Greenland; the furthest is a swallow from South Africa. Volunteers are encouraged to tell
visitors about both.

Nets, poles, bags and the scales live in the ringing store, which is the old coal shed, and go back
there at the end of every session dry, or as dry as the day allows, with wet nets hung on the line
inside rather than stuffed into their bags. A net with a hole is marked with a tag and mended on the
next wet afternoon by whoever can. Bags are washed weekly in the season and hung to dry in the
store.

The tide table on the store door is the ringing team's clock. Nets on the marsh edge are set only on a
falling tide and furled before the flood reaches the boardwalk, and the team leader carries the table
in a pocket and looks at it more often than at the birds. Two volunteers have been caught by the tide
in the observatory's history, both on days when nobody was carrying the table.

Weather stops ringing before it stops anything else. Nets are not opened in rain, in a wind above
force four on the marsh, or in temperatures where a bird held for five minutes would chill, and the
warden's decision on the day is final. Volunteers who have driven a long way for a session that is
called off are thanked and offered the census instead, which goes ahead in anything short of a gale.

Every ringer, licensed or training, signs the register at the start of the session and initials the ledger
for the birds they processed. The register is what the licensing scheme audits and the observatory
has never failed an audit, which is a thing the warden mentions more often than volunteers might
like.

The three hides are the near hide by the cottage, the middle hide at the sluice and the far hide on
the shingle spit, and each is looked after by a named volunteer who checks it weekly, sweeps it,
clears the shutters and reports anything broken. Shutters are closed at dusk by the last person out,
and a shutter left open overnight in winter has twice cost the observatory a hide floor.
